## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Explain** PCA's built-in assumptions and where they break -- it returns **uncorrelated**
  max-variance axes, which is weaker than independence and treats variance as signal -- motivating two
  cousins. *(Understand)*
- **Explain** **Factor Analysis**: a few latent Gaussian **factors** linearly mixed plus **per-feature**
  noise (a generative model fit by EM); PCA is the special case where that noise is equal in every
  feature. *(Understand)*
- **Explain** **ICA**: recovering statistically **independent**, **non-Gaussian** sources from linear
  mixtures (**blind source separation**), a strictly stronger demand than PCA's uncorrelatedness.
  *(Understand)*

  `noise_variance_`, and compare held-out log-likelihood. *(Apply)*

  toolbox map -- linear PCA / FA / ICA versus nonlinear t-SNE / LLE. *(Analyze)*

## Why This Matters

PCA is the right first move for dimensionality reduction, but it answers exactly one question: *which
orthogonal directions hold the most variance?* That is not always the question you have. Sometimes your
features are noisy by very different amounts and you want to separate the shared signal from per-feature
noise. Sometimes several independent processes are **mixed** into every measurement and you want the
processes back, not their blend. PCA cannot do either, because the assumptions that make it fast also
make it blunt. This lesson meets the two classic cousins that relax those assumptions -- **Factor
Analysis** and **Independent Component Analysis** -- and closes Unit VII with a map of the whole
dimensionality-reduction toolbox.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
Three people are talking at once, and three microphones each pick up a different mixture of all three
voices. **PCA** is the sound engineer who can only find the loudest *combined* channels -- still
everyone-at-once, just re-aimed. **ICA** is the engineer who insists each output track be a *separate,
self-contained* voice, and so actually pulls the three speakers apart. The trick that makes it possible:
real voices are **non-Gaussian** (spiky, structured), and ICA hunts for exactly that structure.
:::

## PCA's Three Assumptions

PCA is a single SVD of the centered data, and that speed comes from three baked-in assumptions:

1. **Uncorrelated is good enough.** PCA's components are mutually **uncorrelated** (orthogonal). But
   uncorrelated only removes *linear, second-order* dependence; two signals can be uncorrelated and
   still completely predict each other. **Independence** -- no statistical dependence of any order -- is
   strictly stronger.
2. **Variance equals signal.** PCA keeps the highest-variance directions. If one feature is just loud
   noise, PCA chases it anyway.
3. **The mixing is linear.** PCA projects onto a flat subspace; it cannot follow a curved manifold.

Each cousin relaxes one assumption. **Factor Analysis** drops assumption 2 (it models per-feature noise
instead of equating variance with signal). **ICA** drops assumption 1 (it demands full independence, not
mere decorrelation). **Manifold methods** (t-SNE, LLE) drop assumption 3.

## Factor Analysis

Factor Analysis turns dimensionality reduction into a **generative model**. It says each observed sample
$\mathbf{x}$ (with $p$ features) is built from a few latent **factors** $\mathbf{z}$ (with $k \ll p$),
linearly mixed and then corrupted by noise:

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{z} + \boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, \qquad
\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Psi})
$$

The loading matrix $\mathbf{W}$ ($p \times k$) says how the factors combine into features; the key term
is $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$, the noise covariance, which is **diagonal** -- a *separate* noise variance for
each feature. That single design choice is the whole difference from PCA: **PCA is Factor Analysis with
$\boldsymbol{\Psi} = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$**, one noise level shared by all features. When features really
do have unequal noise, FA can absorb it into $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ and keep $\mathbf{W}$ clean, while PCA
is forced to bend its components toward the noisiest features.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  Z["k latent factors<br/>z ~ N(0, I)"] --> M["linear mix<br/>W z + mu"]
  M --> O["observed features x"]
  E["per-feature noise<br/>eps ~ N(0, Psi), Psi diagonal"] --> O
```

Because the factors $\mathbf{z}$ are hidden, FA is fit by **Expectation-Maximization** -- the same engine
that trained the Gaussian mixture in `L25 — Gaussian Mixtures & EM`. There the latent variable was a
discrete cluster label; here it is a continuous factor vector, but the E-step / M-step rhythm is
identical. FA also gives you a real likelihood, so you can compare models with `.score` (held-out
log-likelihood), as the lab does. In the lab, FA's estimated `noise_variance_` recovers the injected
per-feature noise, and on held-out data it **beats PCA under heteroscedastic noise (-7.85 vs -8.94) and
ties it under equal noise (-9.02 vs -9.03)**.

## Independent Component Analysis

ICA attacks a different problem: **blind source separation**. You observe linear mixtures
$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}$ of some hidden sources $\mathbf{s}$, you do not know the mixing
matrix $\mathbf{A}$ ("blind"), and you want an unmixing matrix $\mathbf{W}$ so that

$$
\hat{\mathbf{s}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}
$$

recovers the original sources. The defining requirement is that the recovered components be statistically
**independent** -- not merely uncorrelated, as PCA delivers, but free of dependence at *every* order.

Independence alone is not quite enough: the catch is **non-Gaussianity**. If the sources were Gaussian,
any rotation of them would look identical (a sum of Gaussians is Gaussian), so the sources could never be
pinned down. ICA works precisely because real signals -- voices, the lab's sine / square / sawtooth --
are **non-Gaussian**, and it searches for the unmixing that makes the outputs *as non-Gaussian as
possible*. That is why the central limit theorem is ICA's friend: a mixture of independent sources is
*more* Gaussian than any single source, so "least Gaussian" points back at the originals.

Two practical consequences: ICA first **whitens** the data (often with a PCA step), and its recovered
sources come out with **no natural order, sign, or scale** -- which is why the lab matches them to the
truth by absolute correlation. In the lab, ICA recovers all three sources at `|corr|` >= **0.997**, while
PCA -- finding orthogonal blends rather than independent sources -- reaches only **0.6-0.8**.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: what a 'component' means in each method (Optional)" collapse="true"}

All three methods write the data as a few directions times coefficients, but "component" means something
different in each:

- **PCA** -- an **uncorrelated** direction of maximum remaining variance. Ordered, orthogonal, and
  unique (up to sign). Answers "where is the spread?"
- **Factor Analysis** -- a **latent Gaussian factor**, recovered together with an explicit per-feature
  noise model. Not unique (the factors can be rotated), because FA only cares about explaining the
  *shared* covariance after noise is removed. Answers "what hidden Gaussian causes drive the features,
  and how noisy is each feature?"
- **ICA** -- a statistically **independent, non-Gaussian source**. Unordered and sign/scale-free.
  Answers "what separate processes were mixed together?"

So PCA decorrelates, FA explains shared variance net of noise, and ICA separates independent causes --
three different jobs that all happen to look like "a matrix of components."
:::

## The Unit VII Toolbox

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  S{"What do you want<br/>from the columns?"}
  S -- "compress / visualize<br/>(linear, max variance)" --> P["PCA"]
  S -- "model unequal per-feature<br/>noise + latent factors" --> F["Factor Analysis"]
  S -- "separate independent<br/>non-Gaussian sources" --> I["ICA"]
  S -- "unfold a curved manifold<br/>for a 2-D picture" --> M["t-SNE / LLE<br/>(nonlinear, named)"]
```

PCA, FA, and ICA are all **linear** -- they multiply the data by a matrix. When the structure is a
curved, twisted **manifold** (a 2-D sheet rolled up in higher dimensions), no single linear projection
can unfold it. **Manifold methods** can: **t-SNE** keeps similar points close to draw a 2-D map (the lab
splits the digits into ten clean islands where PCA's projection overlapped), and **LLE** stitches
together local linear patches. They are powerful for **visualization** but slow, stochastic, and one-way
(you cannot `transform` new points or read off variance), so PCA stays the default and these are the
special-occasion tools.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Using ICA on Gaussian sources.** ICA needs **non-Gaussian** sources to work; on Gaussian data there
  is nothing to separate and the result is meaningless. For Gaussian latent structure, that is FA's job.
- **Expecting ICA components in a fixed order or scale.** They have **no** natural order, sign, or
  magnitude. Always match recovered sources to references by correlation, never by position.
- **Thinking FA is "just PCA".** The difference is the **per-feature** noise term $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$.
  With equal noise they coincide; with unequal noise FA is the better model (and the only one with a
  proper likelihood to check).
- **Forgetting to scale features on different units.** Like PCA, FA and ICA are sensitive to feature
  scale; standardize when units differ.
- **Reaching for t-SNE / LLE to preprocess a model.** They are for **pictures**, not pipelines -- there
  is no stable `transform` for new data. Use PCA (or FA) when a downstream model needs the reduced
  features.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is Factor Analysis just PCA with extra steps?"** -- No. The extra step -- a separate noise variance
per feature -- is the point. It makes FA a proper probabilistic model with a likelihood, and it wins
whenever your features are noisy by different amounts. PCA is the equal-noise special case.

**"When would I actually use ICA?"** -- Separating mixed signals: EEG/MEG brain channels, audio source
separation, removing artifacts (eye blinks) from recordings, financial signal extraction. Anywhere
several independent processes are summed into each measurement.

**"What is t-SNE / LLE, and why only named here?"** -- They are **nonlinear** manifold methods for
**visualizing** high-dimensional data in 2-D. They are wonderful for pictures (the lab's digit islands)
but slow, stochastic, and cannot transform new points, so their mechanics belong to a dedicated treatment;
this lesson uses one as a closing taste.

**"How many factors / components should I pick?"** -- For FA, compare held-out log-likelihood across
candidate $k$ (FA has a real `.score`); for ICA, the number of sources is usually known from the problem
(three microphones, three voices).

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| PCA's limits | uncorrelated (not independent), variance = signal, linear |
| Factor Analysis | latent Gaussian **factors** + **per-feature** noise $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$; generative, fit by EM |
| PCA vs FA | PCA = FA with equal noise ($\boldsymbol{\Psi} = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$); FA wins under unequal noise |
| ICA | un-mix **independent**, **non-Gaussian** sources: $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}$, $\hat{\mathbf{s}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$ |
| Why non-Gaussian | Gaussian sources are rotationally ambiguous; ICA maximizes non-Gaussianity |
| Uncorrelated vs independent | PCA decorrelates (second-order); ICA enforces full independence |
| Blind source separation | recover sources from mixtures with no knowledge of the mixing (the cocktail party) |
| t-SNE / LLE | **nonlinear** manifold methods for **visualization** only (no transform for new points) |
| Toolbox | compress -> PCA; latent factors + unequal noise -> FA; separate sources -> ICA; curved manifold -> t-SNE/LLE |
